notes: "'Bring me a sword,' said the Nutcracker. Fritz gave him a little sword." - the listener of the request is unstated, and Fritz handing the sword straight to the toy differs from A2-C1 (Fritz gives it to Marie). Consider: "'Bring me a sword,' the Nutcracker said to Marie. Fritz gave Marie a little sword."

"'Give me your sweets!' said the Mouse King. Marie gave him her sugar toys." - no reason is given for Marie obeying; a short threat would help, e.g. "He looked at the Nutcracker and showed his teeth."
"candy trees" is American usage while every other level uses British "sweets"; consider "trees full of sweets".

issues.quote: "Give me your sugar toys," whispered the Mouse King. "Or I bite your Nutcracker!"
issues.problem: A native writer would never phrase a threat as "Or I bite your Nutcracker!"; the present simple here is a calque forced by the tense restriction and teaches learners a wrong pattern.
issues.fix: Show the threat without future tense: "Give me your sugar toys," whispered the Mouse King, and he showed his sharp teeth to the Nutcracker.

issues.quote: 3. How did Marie and the Nutcracker get to the Doll Kingdom? — Through the glass cupboard / In a golden carriage / *Through the sleeve of her father's coat
issues.problem: The distractor "In a golden carriage" is defensible: the same text says the young man, who is the Nutcracker, "came for her in a golden carriage" and Marie is now queen of the Doll Kingdom.
issues.fix: Replace the distractor with one not in the story, e.g. "On a toy horse", or ask "How did Marie and the Nutcracker get to the Doll Kingdom the first time?"

notes: "Hundreds of mice were coming out from the cracks in the floor." - after "Soon the big clock struck twelve" a sudden event reads better in past simple: "Hundreds of mice came out of the cracks in the floor."
"You played with your toys too late," said her mother. - slightly unidiomatic; "You stayed up too late playing with your toys."

"He must win against the Mouse King, the son of the mouse queen. Also, a girl must love him." - "He must beat the Mouse King, the son of the mouse queen. And a girl must love him." sounds more natural.
"In that instant the whole army vanished" - could be read as both armies; "the whole mouse army vanished" is clearer.
"Her mother explained that she had stayed up far too late and had a bad dream." - "had had a bad dream" or "had only been dreaming" keeps the backshift consistent.

"If you were real, I would never laugh at you like that princess did." "I would love you just as you are," she added. - "real" is confusing when Marie believes he is real; "alive" or "a real person" is clearer, and the two-part quote with "she added" is clunky; merge into one speech.
"Behind the glass, the cupboard came alive." - acceptable figuratively, but "Behind the glass, the toys in the cupboard came alive" avoids a momentary misreading.
"the courteous nephew cracked their nuts for them" - consider "cracked nuts for the children" to avoid any adult double reading.

summary: A faithful, gentle retelling of Hoffmann's tale (not the ballet): the glass wig, the owl, the left slipper, the Pirlipat tale with the bacon, the colonel's sword, the coat sleeve, the watch-chain crowns and the golden carriage are all correct, and nothing breaks the 4+ rating. B1, B2 and C1 pass with minor style notes. A2 fails on one unnatural threat line forced by the tense limit and on a quiz distractor that the story itself makes defensible.
